port.subsystem: Data layer, sync, and background execution (encrypted DB, token storage, HTTP backend surface, auth flows, polling orchestration, background execution model, boot restart, retention, in-app update, backend-optional local-only mode)

ports_cleanly.capability: Encrypted local database (SQLCipher + Room) → SQLCipher + GRDB.swift
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: SQLCipher is fully supported on iOS. Use GRDB.swift compiled against SQLCipher (GRDB is the only mature Swift layer that gives the SQL-level control this schema needs: UNIQUE indexes, INSERT OR IGNORE vs OR REPLACE conflict clauses, the single-query time-in-range aggregate, and a multi-table DELETE in one transaction — Core Data can express none of those and is not supported on an encrypted store). GRDB's DatabaseMigrator replaces Room migrations, and GRDB's ValueObservation replaces Room's observable queries 1:1. Two important substitutions: (1) the 32-byte SecureRandom passphrase moves from EncryptedSharedPreferences to a Keychain kSecClassGenericPassword item with kSecAttrAccessible = kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly — NOT WhenUnlocked, or every background wake after a screen lock fails to open the DB and the alert floor silently dies; (2) the database file must be set to FileProtectionType.completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication for the same reason. Keep the fail-loud posture: a failed Keychain write throws rather than minting a second key. The Android migration chain 6→13 does NOT need porting — a fresh iOS install creates the v13 schema directly; migrations 6→13 matter only as documentation of the final shape (unique index on cgm_readings.timestampMs and basal_readings.timestampMs, source/category/ack_synced columns with their defaults). Room's fallbackToDestructiveMigration has no GRDB equivalent and should not be recreated: write explicit migrations and fail loudly instead. Info.plist needs ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption declared so TestFlight uploads don't prompt on every build.

ports_cleanly.capability: Room entities and DAO surface (nine tables, query limits, ordering, time-in-range aggregation, defensive entity→domain mapping)
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: Direct port to GRDB records + a repository type. All nine tables, all indexes, all conflict strategies (REPLACE vs IGNORE per DAO method), all LIMIT/ORDER semantics, and the observeTimeInRangeCounts single-query aggregate translate to SQL verbatim. Kotlin Flow → GRDB ValueObservation exposed as AsyncSequence or Combine publisher. The defensive mapping (unknown activityMode → NONE, unknown trend → UNKNOWN, out-of-safety-range rows returning nil and being dropped by mapNotNull) becomes a failable init plus compactMap. Swift's failable initializers are a better fit than Kotlin's require+try/catch: model the 20…500 mg/dL and 0…25 U bounds as init? returning nil rather than throwing.

Pure SQL and pure logic; ports verbatim including the exponential-backoff selection predicate (lastAttemptMs < now - 2000 * (1 << retryCount)), the pending/sending/failed vocabulary, markTransientFailure's deliberate non-increment, resetStaleSending's 60s reclaim, pruneOldest excluding in-flight rows, and cleanup's retry+age cutoff. Because eligibility is already a SQL predicate over stored timestamps rather than an in-memory timer, this design survives iOS's irregular background schedule without modification — that is the single most fortunate property of the existing design.

Pure mapping plus one batch insert in a transaction. Moshi adapter → Codable encoder. Preserve the two load-bearing behaviours exactly: the backend-configured gate is read ONCE per call (not per event), and the whole body swallows every error except cancellation so an enqueue failure can never kill the poll loop. In Swift, express the latter as a non-throwing method that logs; make the poll loop physically unable to see the error. Keep the wire quirks: IoB uploads as event_type "bg_reading" with iob_at_event, basal duplicates pump_activity_mode into control_iq_mode for tolerant older backends, and CGM is never enqueued.

ports_cleanly.capability: Raw pump history log storage and upload
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: Direct port. UNIQUE index on sequenceNumber with INSERT OR IGNORE, getUnsent(limit:100), markSent, getMaxSequenceNumber as the poller's resume anchor, and deleteAllButMaxSequence for stand-down. Swift's Int is 64-bit so the unsigned-32-bit-sequence-stored-as-signed-Int concern disappears entirely. Fix the observed gap while porting: wire the cleanup(cutoffMs) call that has zero production callers on Android, so raw_history_logs is bounded in full-stack mode too.

EncryptedSharedPreferences 'auth_credentials' → six Keychain generic-password items (or one JSON blob) with kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly. Base URL is not a secret and can live in UserDefaults, which also solves the reactive signal. The SharedPreferences change-listener callbackFlow has no Keychain equivalent — but it never needed one: all writes are in-process, so publish an AsyncStream/CurrentValueSubject from the store itself on every write, and seed it from the stored value at construction. Keep the register-before-read ordering property by making the subject the single source (write → subject.send). JWT exp extraction (split on '.', Base64URL-decode part 1, regex for "exp", ×1000, any failure → 0 = assume valid) is a few lines of Swift. Preserve the deliberate quirks: getToken() returns nil past expiry without clearing; isRefreshTokenExpired treats unknown expiry as valid; clearToken preserves the base URL. ONE NEW REQUIREMENT iOS forces: Keychain items survive app deletion, so a reinstall would inherit a previous install's tokens, pump pairing secret and DB passphrase against a database file that no longer exists. Detect first-run-after-install via a UserDefaults sentinel and purge the app's Keychain items before anything reads them.

ports_cleanly.capability: AuthRepository — login/logout and per-account settings reconcile
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: Pure orchestration over HTTP; ports verbatim. Preserve the validation ordering, the six fire-and-forget post-login fetches, and every safety-critical validation rule unchanged: glucose range requires strict ordering and 20…500 after rounding; alert thresholds validate strict ordering on the RAW floats before rounding; safety limits reject min>=max / min not in 20…499 / max not in 21…500 / basal not in 1…15000 / bolus not in 1…25000; meal-intelligence 401/403 fails closed to false. One improvement the port should make: run the post-login fetches on a task tied to the app, not the screen, so backgrounding the login screen mid-flight doesn't cancel them (the Android version's caller-scope bug). Logout ordering (bump generation → clear token → clear stores → best-effort deregister, base URL preserved) ports as-is.

URLSession + Codable behind a generated-or-hand-written endpoint enum. Retrofit's Response<T> semantics (all HTTP statuses are values, only transport failures throw) map to returning (Data, HTTPURLResponse) and throwing only on URLError — this is actually the natural URLSession shape. Moshi's ignore-unknown-keys is Codable's default. Two concrete gotchas to legislate against: (a) Swift Codable does NOT apply a property's default value when a key is absent — Moshi's Kotlin adapter does — so every field with a Kotlin default (is_automated=false, acknowledged=false, raw_accepted=0, raw_duplicates=0, source="mobile") must use decodeIfPresent ?? default or the whole response fails to parse; (b) ISO_INSTANT accepts fractional seconds and ISO8601DateFormatter with .withInternetDateTime alone does not, so the date strategy must accept both forms. Multipart food-record upload → hand-built multipart body via URLSession upload task. The 15/90/10-second timeout profiles become three URLSession instances; the chat client's isolated Dispatcher+ConnectionPool becomes its own URLSession with httpMaximumConnectionsPerHost set.

ports_cleanly.capability: OkHttp client construction and interceptor chain
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: URLSession has no interceptor chain, so the ordered chain becomes an explicit layered async client — and since the app owns every call site, this is simpler than the Android version, not harder. Layers in the same load-bearing order: (1) resolve base URL, throwing the same two distinct configuration errors and re-applying the transport policy as defense in depth; (2) attach Bearer token, omitting the header entirely when the token is expired; (3) on 401, one serialized refresh-and-retry (Swift actor replaces runBlocking + Mutex, and is strictly better — no thread blocking); (4) record reachability success/failure around only the real network call, excluding cancelled tasks; (5) debug fault injection; (6) logging. Keep the chat/LLM session excluded from the reachability signal. Note only the request's scheme/host/port are rewritten — preserve that (and the known gap that a path prefix in the user's base URL is dropped) or fix it deliberately, not accidentally.

ConnectivityManager.registerDefaultNetworkCallback → NWPathMonitor. path.status == .satisfied is the right analog of NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET-without-VALIDATED: a LAN-only Wi-Fi with no internet still reports satisfied, which is exactly what a self-hosted backend needs. Seed pessimistically from currentPath before the first update, same as the Android seed. The backend-reachability half (2 consecutive transport failures, atomic counter, reset on any response including 4xx/5xx, cancelled calls excluded) is pure logic and ports verbatim; use an actor instead of AtomicInteger. Expose the same three-state precedence (offline > backend-unreachable > reachable) and the same reconcile-acks-on-REACHABLE trigger.

ports_cleanly.capability: Alert persistence and offline acknowledgement reconcile
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: Direct port. The alerts table with UNIQUE server_id, the two-field acknowledged/ack_synced model, insertPreservingLocalAck as a transaction that refuses to let a server echo downgrade a local ack, TERMINAL_ACK_CODES {403,404,422}, the Mutex-serialized reconcile that bails on the first IOException, and pushing deferred acks before pulling — all pure logic. Swift actor replaces the Mutex. Reconcile triggers change only in name: NetworkMonitor transition to reachable, app activation, every background execution opportunity, and completion of a background upload. Fix the observed gap: run the 7-day alert cleanup on a schedule the user can't opt out of by never opening the alerts screen.

ports_cleanly.capability: Local settings stores (SharedPreferences layer, nine stores)
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: Plain stores → UserDefaults; encrypted stores → Keychain (auth_credentials, pump_credentials incl. JPAKE secrets, db passphrase) with AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly. All listener-backed flows become in-process publishers. Keep AlertThresholdStore and GlucoseRangeStore as two separate stores with separate semantics — the identical 55/70/180/250 defaults make merging them tempting and it would alarm at display-range values. Keep requireSafeThresholds and SafetyLimits.safeOf clamping. Two iOS-specific changes: (1) the .commit() vs .apply() durability distinction has no UserDefaults analog (synchronize() is a deprecated no-op), so put the safety-critical stores — alert thresholds and safety limits — in the encrypted database or an atomically-written file rather than UserDefaults, preserving the fail-loud-and-keep-old-values behaviour; (2) AlertSoundStore's entire channel-version machinery disappears because iOS has no notification channels and sound is a per-notification property — but iOS also cannot use an arbitrary system ringtone: custom sounds must be bundled with the app (or in Library/Sounds) and under 30 seconds, so the sound picker becomes a fixed list of bundled sounds plus Default and Silent. The watchface_* settings keys become complication/widget configuration (watchOS has no custom watch faces).

Pure logic; ports verbatim including every one of the seven behaviours: enqueuer returns early, sync manager stands down and sweeps hourly, backend requests fail before touching the network, cloud-source sync stands down while retaining its activation flag, local alert-threshold editing is offered only while no backend exists, clearBaseUrl also clears backend thresholds, and the coverage copy uses the no-server phrasing. This mode is MORE important on iOS than on Android: without a backend there is no push path at all, so the on-device floor is unambiguously the only alerting, and the copy must say so. It is also the only posture that needs no Local Network permission and no ATS exception.

POST /api/v1/devices/register with platform "ios" — already in the contract's enum (verified: ["android","ios","wear"]), and build_type maps to the existing ["debug","release"] enum. Three field substitutions: device_token stays a locally generated UUID for bookkeeping (and becomes the APNs token only if push is adopted); device_fingerprint = SHA-256 of identifierForVendor + bundle identifier, dropping the signing-certificate hash which has no practical iOS equivalent; device_name cannot be the user-assigned device name — since iOS 16 UIDevice.current.name returns the model string unless you hold the com.apple.developer.device-information.user-assigned-device-name entitlement, so send the model plus a short install-scoped suffix so two iPhones are distinguishable in the device list. The Apple Watch should not register separately — it has no independent server-alert delivery path.

GlycemicGptApp.onCreate → SwiftUI App init / UIApplicationDelegate didFinishLaunching, in the same order: logging first, crash reporting second, retention scheduling, network monitor start with pessimistic seed, ack-reconcile subscriber on the reachability stream, driver registry (now compile-time-linked modules registered into a static list rather than a plugin registry), auth startup validation on an app-lifetime task, then pump connection start if paired. The app-lifetime CoroutineScope becomes a retained Task or an actor-owned task group. Register BGTaskScheduler handlers here — Apple requires all handlers registered before didFinishLaunching returns, which is a hard ordering constraint the Android version doesn't have.

ports_cleanly.capability: Logging, scrubbing, and crash reporting posture
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: Timber → OSLog (or swift-log) with a release policy of warning-and-above and the same four scrubbing regexes applied before emission (JWT-shaped token, email, N mg/dL, N.N mmol/L), keeping Locale.US-equivalent formatting so mmol output still matches the scrubber. Sentry has a Cocoa SDK with the same beforeSend/beforeBreadcrumb hooks, so the entire locked-down posture ports: no PII, no screenshots, no view hierarchy, no session tracking, zero traces/profiles sample rate, breadcrumb category dropping, IP set to 0.0.0.0, serverName/request/timezone/locale nulled, and message/exception/breadcrumb/tag scrubbing. Keep the DSN-empty-in-CI rule. ONE ADDITION iOS forces: the Android release posture relies on logcat being the client-side diagnostic trail, and iOS gives users no equivalent — so the app must keep a bounded in-app log buffer with a scrubbed share/export action, otherwise a TestFlight user reporting a bug has nothing to send.

ports_cleanly.capability: Backend contract pinning and compatibility posture
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: Vendor contract/openapi.json byte-for-byte and CONTRACT_VERSION alongside the Swift package, and port ContractSmokeTest to XCTest: round-trip spec-conforming payloads through the real Codable types, assert unknown fields are ignored, assert a renamed/removed consumed field fails to decode, and assert every endpoint the client calls exists in the pinned spec's paths. Port SafetyConstantDriftGuardTest including its comment-stripped source scan of every duplication site. ADR 0001's decision not to normalize endpoint versioning carries over unchanged. The Codable-no-implicit-defaults hazard makes the smoke test MORE valuable on iOS than on Android, because a backend that stops sending an optional-with-default field breaks Swift where it would not break Moshi — the test must specifically assert every defaulted field decodes correctly when absent.

needs_redesign.capability: BackendSyncManager — the 3-second queue drain loop, stand-down, and hygiene
needs_redesign.why: The entire lifecycle is a coroutine loop that lives inside a foreground service and wakes every 3 seconds forever. iOS has no foreground service and suspends the app within seconds of backgrounding; no timer, loop or delay executes while suspended. A push started in the foreground is also killed at suspension unless it is on a background URLSession. Separately, the retry timings (2s/4s/8s/16s/32s, budget exhausted in ~62s) and the 60-second stale-sending reclaim assume a drain opportunity every few seconds, which iOS will not provide.
options: Keep the loop verbatim but only while the app is foregrounded, and accept that background sync stops entirely — honest, simple, and the queue drains on next activation. Loses nothing except upload freshness.

Drive the drain from execution opportunities instead of a timer: app activation, every Core Bluetooth wake (each BLE callback is an execution window — the enqueue and the drain kick both fit), BGAppRefreshTask (~30s of runtime, system-scheduled, earliestBeginDate is a floor not a guarantee), BGProcessingTask for the hourly hygiene, and the background-URLSession completion relaunch. Because getPendingBatch is already a SQL predicate over stored timestamps, sparse opportunities delay delivery without corrupting state.

Perform the actual HTTP push on a background URLSession (URLSessionConfiguration.background) so an upload survives suspension and termination and relaunches the app on completion. Constraint: background sessions support only upload/download tasks with a file-backed body, so each batch must be serialized to a temp file and uploaded via uploadTask(with:fromFile:); the system may also mark it discretionary and defer it.
Adopt silent remote notifications (content-available) to trigger drains — rejected: requires push infrastructure the backend does not have, and iOS budgets background pushes to roughly 2-3/hour.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Do all three of the first options together. Foreground: run the existing 3s loop unchanged so the behaviour the user sees while using the app is identical to Android. Background: replace the loop with an opportunity-driven drain triggered by app activation, every Core Bluetooth wake, BGAppRefreshTask and BGProcessingTask, and push over a background URLSession with the batch written to a temp file. Keep every piece of the queue's logic byte-identical — the retry classification (408/429/502-504 and transport failures do not increment retryCount), markTransientFailure, resetStaleSending, prune-oldest-at-cap, and the hourly cleanup — because that logic is opportunity-agnostic. Two parameter changes are required: raise MAX_QUEUE_SIZE well above 5000 (at the 15s fast cadence the enqueue rate is ~8 rows/min, so 5000 rows is ~10 hours, and an iPhone that cannot drain for longer than that would silently discard the oldest pump history), and lengthen the stale-sending reclaim beyond 60 seconds since a background-URLSession push legitimately takes longer than that. Keep the reactive backend-configured lifecycle (configured → drain, unconfigured → hourly stand-down purge) driven by the same in-process signal; on iOS the stand-down sweep runs on the same opportunity schedule rather than an hourly timer.

needs_redesign.capability: PumpPollingOrchestrator — poll cadences, keep-alive, and history backfill
needs_redesign.why: Three concurrent forever-loops at 15s / 5min / 5min, all inside a foreground service holding a wake lock. On iOS: no wake lock exists, no timer fires while suspended, and the 15-second cadence exists specifically because the pump drops idle BLE connections at ~30 seconds — which means a suspended iOS app will lose the link and be dependent on reconnection. The backfill deadlines (2 minutes normal, 20 minutes initial sync) exceed every background execution window iOS offers; BGProcessingTask can run for minutes but only when the system chooses, typically while charging and idle.
options: Foreground: identical loops. Background: issue the poll burst inside each Core Bluetooth callback window, which requires the pump to notify (peripheral-initiated) rather than only respond to host-initiated reads. If the pump's protocol is strictly request/response with no notify characteristic, background cadence collapses to whatever wake CoreBluetooth grants on reconnect.

Use CBCentralManager state restoration (CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey + the bluetooth-central background mode) plus a pending connect() with no timeout, so iOS relaunches the app into the background when the peripheral reappears and re-establishes the link without the app running.

Run the initial full-history sync as a foreground, user-visible, cancellable, resumable task with the idle timer disabled, rather than as background work. The sequence-number anchor already makes it resumable.

Use iOS 26's BGContinuedProcessingTask for the initial backfill: it is designed for user-initiated long-running work and shows system progress UI, which fits a 20-minute multi-month history download better than any other API. It is not available for unattended periodic work.
Extend each wake with beginBackgroundTask(expirationHandler:) — buys on the order of 30 seconds, not the 180 seconds older documentation implies.
Take extra wake opportunities from HealthKit observer background delivery if a CGM app writes glucose to HealthKit — real but out-of-band, and rate-limited.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Foreground behaviour is identical to Android — keep all cadence constants, the 500ms request stagger, the 3x low-power multiplier, and the loop composition. Background behaviour must be redesigned around Core Bluetooth as the clock: adopt state restoration and a permanently pending connect(), and run the fast-loop poll burst inside each callback window. Move the low-battery multiplier off ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED (which has no iOS analog while backgrounded) onto ProcessInfo.isLowPowerModeEnabled and its change notification — a better signal anyway, since it is the user's explicit statement of intent. Drop the wake-lock and the <5%-battery release entirely; there is nothing to release. Run the initial history backfill as a foreground task with a progress UI and idle timer disabled, backed by BGContinuedProcessingTask so it survives a brief backgrounding, and keep the anti-stall guard, the sequence anchor, and the 1-second inter-batch stagger unchanged. State plainly in the PRD that background poll cadence is best-effort and that a suspended iPhone may miss readings the Android build would have captured.

needs_redesign.capability: AuthManager — proactive scheduled refresh and the refresh state machine
needs_redesign.why: The state machine, the single refresh mutex shared by the proactive timer and the reactive 401 path, the sessionGeneration logout-race guard, and the five-outcome taxonomy are pure logic that port perfectly (and a Swift actor is a better fit than Mutex + @Volatile). What does not port is the scheduling: scheduleRefresh computes a delay to five minutes before expiry and sleeps on an app-lifetime scope. On iOS that Task cannot run while the app is suspended, so a token expiring overnight is never proactively refreshed, and the TRANSIENT_RETRY_DELAY_MS = 60_000 reschedule loop is equally dead.
options: Keep the timer for foreground only and add a refresh-if-expiring-soon check at every execution opportunity (app activation, scene foregrounding, each Core Bluetooth wake, each BG task, and immediately before any queued network call).

Rely purely on the reactive 401 path and drop proactive refresh — rejected: a background upload that 401s on a background URLSession cannot easily replay after an async refresh, and the whole point of the 5-minute window is to avoid that.
Schedule a BGAppRefreshTask near expiry — unreliable as the sole mechanism, useful as an extra opportunity.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Port the state machine, the actor-serialized refresh, the generation counter, the outcome taxonomy and every documented invariant unchanged (Expired preserves the store, Rejected clears the token, Discarded touches nothing, ServerError/NetworkFailure preserve tokens and keep the session Authenticated on a stale token rather than showing a false session-expired banner, logout always wins). Replace the timer with opportunity-driven refresh: check isTokenExpiringSoon(5 min) at app activation, on every background execution opportunity, and as a precondition of enqueuing a background upload — the last one matters most, because a background URLSession upload must carry a token that will still be valid when the system decides to run it. Keep the foreground timer as an optimization only. Keep performRefreshWithRetry's 1s/2s backoff and its rule that exhaustion only flips to Expired when there is genuinely no token.

needs_redesign.why: The pure classifier (literal-IP-only, no DNS lookup, strict IPv4 octet parsing rejecting octal/hex/decimal encodings, hand-written IPv6 with one :: and %zone stripping, the .local mDNS exception) ports verbatim to Swift. But the enforcement stack around it changes materially and gains a gate Android has no analog for. iOS App Transport Security replaces network_security_config with different expressiveness, and iOS 14+ requires an explicit Local Network privacy grant before an app may contact any host on the local network — a denial produces connection failures that look like a dead server, not a permission error. Additionally, the Android debug affordance of allowing http:// to ANY host is not available in a TestFlight build without NSAllowsArbitraryLoads, which is review-visible.
options: Info.plist NSAppTransportSecurity with NSAllowsLocalNetworking = YES only. This permits cleartext to private/link-local IP literals, .local names and unqualified hostnames while still forbidding cleartext to public hosts — remarkably close to isPrivateHost, and Apple treats it as an exception that needs no review justification.
Add NSAllowsArbitraryLoads for the debug configuration only, via a separate Info.plist per build configuration, so the shipping/TestFlight binary never carries it.
Keep UrlSecurityPolicy enforcing the same rule in code at both save time and request time, as defense in depth, exactly as today — ATS is a second, independent gate, not a replacement.
Add NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription and an explicit permission flow with a Settings deep link on denial; optionally declare NSBonjourServices if .local browsing is used.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Ship NSAllowsLocalNetworking = YES in the release Info.plist and NSAllowsArbitraryLoads only in a debug-configuration Info.plist. Keep the pure policy in Swift, enforced at both save and request time as today, and do not weaken it to rely on ATS — ATS's exact CIDR coverage should be treated as unverified and the in-code classifier as authoritative. Add explicit Local Network permission handling with a purpose string, a pre-flight probe, and a distinct user-facing error ('Local Network access is off for this app') so a denied grant is never reported as a generic network failure. Note one iOS advantage worth stating in the PRD: unlike Android 7+, iOS apps trust user-installed CA certificates by default, so a self-hoster with a private CA can use https:// without any app change — this is a materially better path than the LAN-HTTP opt-in and should be the recommended setup.

needs_redesign.capability: On-device alert floor gates that the data layer feeds
needs_redesign.why: The classification, freshness policy, wall-clock rewind high-water mark, cooldown, episode guard and ack-gated re-arm are pure logic that port perfectly. Three of the four arming preconditions change meaning on iOS. Gate 1 (server alerting degraded) is derived from the SSE stream's state — but a persistent SSE connection cannot exist while an iOS app is suspended, so in the background the floor would be permanently armed, inverting the primary dedup layer. Gate 4 (POST_NOTIFICATIONS granted) becomes a much sharper question: to actually alarm through silent mode and Focus, iOS requires the Critical Alerts entitlement (com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts), which is granted only by an approved request to Apple; without it a low-glucose alarm is silent whenever the ringer is off. And the floor only fires at all if the app is executing, which on iOS means a Core Bluetooth wake happened.
options: Apply for the Critical Alerts entitlement — Apple grants it to diabetes/medical monitoring apps and it is what Dexcom, Loop and similar use. Grants UNAuthorizationOptions.criticalAlert, UNNotificationSound.criticalSoundNamed(_:withAudioVolume:), and bypass of both the ringer switch and Focus.

Fall back to the Time Sensitive interruption level (com.apple.developer.usernotifications.time-sensitive, freely enabled in Xcode) which breaks through Focus but NOT the silent switch — and say so in the UI rather than implying an alarm that cannot sound.

Redefine gate 1 for iOS: treat 'server alerting degraded' as true whenever the app has no live server alert channel, and rely on the existing 30-minute cooldown, the shared stable notification slot, and the ack-gated episode guard (which reads the server's own alert history from the DB) to suppress double-alarming when the server later delivers the same alert.
Retain the SSE stream only while the app is foregrounded, so gate 1 behaves exactly like Android's while the user is looking at the app.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Port the floor's logic unchanged — same classify order (urgent first), same FreshnessPolicy (CGM 6/15 min, pump 15/60 min, debug 20/45 s), same ALERT_FLOOR_MAX_FUTURE_SKEW_MS = 60_000, same monotonic wall-clock high-water mark suppressing both firing and the watching claim, same 30-minute cooldown mirroring the server's dedup window, same ack-gated episode guard clamped with min(recentServerAlert, now), same fail-toward-alerting on a failed episode lookup. Redefine gate 1 as 'no live server alert channel' and lean harder on the episode guard, which already reads Room's server-alert history and is the mechanism that makes this safe. Apply for the Critical Alerts entitlement as a launch blocker for the alarm feature, ship Time Sensitive as the fallback, and make the app's honesty surface state which one is active — 'alarms will sound even when silenced' vs 'alarms will not sound while your iPhone is silenced'. Note plainly that the floor can only fire while the app has execution time, so a suspended app with no Bluetooth wake produces no floor alarm at all — this is the honest ceiling of iOS background monitoring.

needs_redesign.capability: CGM watch relay and alert-floor hand-off (processCgmReading)
needs_redesign.why: The relay's decision logic — one classification feeding both consumers, the isReadingAlertable data-trust gate that skips the ENTIRE alert block (no send, no clear, latch untouched), recovery keyed on the classification being in range rather than on a null mapping, the 5-minute silent refresh, the 30-minute rebuzz matching FLOOR_COOLDOWN_MS, and mutex serialization across the poll loop / manual refresh / debug injector — is pure logic and ports perfectly to a Swift actor. What changes is the transport and the meaning of 'buzz the wrist'. Wear DataLayer becomes WatchConnectivity, which has different delivery classes and budgets, and there is no way to make the Watch vibrate from the phone other than a notification.
options: WCSession.updateApplicationContext for latest-state CGM/coverage (coalesced, delivered in background, replaces DataItem semantics exactly); transferUserInfo for FIFO-ordered items that must not be dropped; sendMessage only when isReachable for immediate foreground updates; transferCurrentComplicationUserInfo for high-priority complication pushes, which carries a limited daily budget (historically 50/day).

Replace the custom wrist alert entirely with iPhone notification mirroring: iOS forwards notifications to a paired Watch when the iPhone is locked, and watchOS renders the watch app's notification interface with haptics. The 30-minute rebuzz becomes re-posting the notification; the 5-minute silent refresh becomes an applicationContext update.
Make the watchOS app fetch alerts from the backend independently when a backend is configured, so the wrist is not solely dependent on phone relay.
Keep a watch-side local decay so the Watch ages its own copy out on its own clock rather than trusting an unbounded-stale relay.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Keep the relay's logic verbatim in an actor. Send state (glucose, trend, timestamp, thresholds, unit, coverage claim) via updateApplicationContext, which matches DataItem semantics closely enough that the existing wire contract survives. Deliver the wrist ALERT as an iPhone local notification and let watchOS mirror it — this collapses the Android design's careful three-path deduplication into one path and is strictly simpler, and it also means the wrist alarm inherits whatever critical-alert capability the phone has. Preserve exactly the two properties that make the Android relay safe: a not-alertable reading skips the whole alert block rather than clearing, and recovery is keyed on the classification being in range so a mapping gap can cost a push but never produce a false 'All clear'. Keep watch-side freshness decay so the Watch degrades to 'stale' on its own clock; do not let it render a relayed value as current indefinitely.

needs_redesign.why: WorkManager's guaranteed periodic execution has no iOS equivalent. BGProcessingTask is discretionary — the system decides when, typically while charging and idle, and may skip days for an app the user opens rarely. ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP and the HiltWorkerFactory/manual-initialization machinery are Android-only concerns that simply disappear.
options: Register a BGProcessingTaskRequest and treat it as an optimization, not a guarantee.

Run the retention delete opportunistically: on every app foreground and on every background execution opportunity. The query is a single indexed DELETE across six tables in one transaction — cheap enough to run every time without a throttle beyond a once-per-hour guard.
Enforce retention lazily at read time (filter by cutoff in queries) so an unpruned DB never surfaces stale data even if the delete has not run.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Do the opportunistic version as the primary mechanism and register a BGProcessingTask as a supplement. Keep the 1/7/30-day setting with the same coercion, and keep the single-transaction six-table delete. While porting, close the two observed retention gaps: the alert table's 7-day cleanup must not depend on the user opening the alerts screen, and raw_history_logs must actually be pruned in full-stack mode (the Android cleanup(cutoffMs) has zero production callers), because on iOS an unbounded table competes for a storage budget the system can reclaim under pressure.

needs_redesign.why: The engine — connection resolution honouring an explicit selection only while active, 500-per-array paging, the inclusive cursor relying on idempotent inserts for boundary dedup, the min-of-full-streams cursor advance, the saturated-boundary transient throw, the AuthError-does-not-retry classification, and the whole NightscoutDataMapper validation set including the deliberate combo_bolus exclusion — is pure logic that ports verbatim. Only the scheduler changes: WorkManager's 15-minute periodic floor with a NetworkType.CONNECTED constraint has no iOS equivalent with comparable reliability.
options: BGAppRefreshTask with earliestBeginDate 15 minutes out, re-scheduled after each run — opportunistic, realistically a handful to a few dozen runs per day depending on how often the user opens the app.
Run on every app foreground and on every other background execution opportunity, which the design already tolerates because each run fully backfills from the cursor.
Rely on the phone being awake for BLE anyway and piggyback on Core Bluetooth wakes.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Register a BGAppRefreshTask and additionally run the sync on app foreground and on every background wake. The Android design explicitly documents that a faster source interval never loses data — it only changes freshness — so a sparse iOS schedule degrades gracefully by construction. Keep the per-connection cursor, the paging loop, the cursor-advance rule, the NoBackend backstop for a run racing a mode flip, and the row-count-only logging discipline unchanged. Surface last-sync time and status in the UI so the user can see freshness rather than assuming a 15-minute cadence that iOS will not deliver.

impossible.capability: PumpConnectionService — a foreground service with a persistent ongoing notification, a PARTIAL_WAKE_LOCK, and START_STICKY restart
impossible.why: iOS has no foreground services, no user-dismissable-but-persistent ongoing notification tied to a running process, no wake locks, and no mechanism for the system to restart a killed app. An app is suspended within seconds of leaving the foreground and executes only when the system wakes it. There is no API — public or entitled — that keeps an iOS app running continuously. The battery-driven policy is equally unavailable: ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED has no background analog, and UIDevice.batteryLevel only updates while the app runs.
impossible.closest_alternative: Three surfaces together, none of which is permanent. (1) Core Bluetooth's bluetooth-central background mode with CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey state restoration keeps the CONNECTION alive across suspension and lets iOS relaunch the app into the background for peripheral events — this replaces the wake lock's actual purpose (the system holds the link instead of the app holding the CPU) and is in one respect better than Android. (2) For the honest-coverage notification text: a Live Activity (ActivityKit) on the Lock Screen and Dynamic Island, updated from the app whenever it has execution time — but it is capped at roughly 8 hours active (plus a few hours lingering in Notification Center), is user-dismissable, and cannot be recreated without the app running, so it cannot be the permanent honesty surface the Android notification is. (3) A Home Screen / Lock Screen WidgetKit widget showing last reading, its age, and the coverage claim, reloaded via WidgetCenter.reloadTimelines on every execution opportunity; unattended timeline refreshes are budgeted (roughly tens per day) but a widget that shows a timestamp degrades honestly on its own. Replace the battery policy with ProcessInfo.isLowPowerModeEnabled. Do NOT use the audio background mode or a silent-audio keepalive to stay running — Apple rejects it and it would fail Beta App Review.

impossible.capability: BootCompletedReceiver — automatic restart after device reboot
impossible.why: iOS has no launch-at-boot for third-party apps and no broadcast an app can subscribe to. Apple's documented rule for Core Bluetooth state restoration is that the system does not relaunch an app the user force-quit, and after a device restart the app must be launched by the user before restoration applies. There is no code path by which the app can notice a reboot happened, because no code runs.
impossible.closest_alternative: Core Bluetooth state restoration covers the case the Android receiver does NOT cover — relaunch after the system terminates the app to reclaim memory — but not reboot or force-quit. The only honest mitigations are product ones: tell the user during onboarding that monitoring stops after a restart until the app is opened; keep a Home Screen widget whose displayed data age makes a stopped app visibly obvious; and, when the app does launch, detect a long gap since the last recorded reading and surface it. If a backend and push are adopted, a server-side watchdog noticing that a device stopped pushing could send a push that relaunches the app into the background — that is the only mechanism that can restart monitoring without the user, and it requires the push infrastructure the backend does not currently have.

impossible.capability: Persistent server-alert stream (AlertStreamService's foreground-service SSE connection)
impossible.why: A long-lived HTTP connection cannot be held open by a suspended iOS app, and there is no background mode that permits it. URLSession background configurations support only upload and download tasks — not streaming data tasks — so SSE cannot be moved there either. Verified against the repo: contract/openapi.json contains no APNs, FCM or push-token endpoint of any kind; server alerts reach the device only via GET /api/v1/alerts/stream or GET /api/v1/alerts/pending. So today there is no mechanism by which a backgrounded iPhone can receive a server-generated alert.
impossible.closest_alternative: Apple Push Notification service is the only path, and it requires a new backend capability (an APNs sender) plus an APNs auth key scoped to the app's bundle identifier. Without push: run the SSE stream only while the app is foregrounded, pull /api/v1/alerts/pending at every execution opportunity, and treat the on-device alert floor as the sole background alerting mechanism — which raises the stakes on the Critical Alerts entitlement considerably. Note that background alert PULLING is also weak: BGAppRefreshTask cadence is opportunistic, so a pull-only design cannot promise timely delivery of a server alert.

impossible.capability: In-app update checking and APK self-install (AppUpdateChecker, REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES, FileProvider install intent)
impossible.why: iOS forbids an app from downloading and executing or installing code. There is no FileProvider install intent, no ACTION_VIEW for a package, and no sideload path within a TestFlight-distributed app. The entire download/size-check/host-allowlist/sanitize/install pipeline has no target.
impossible.closest_alternative: Keep the GitHub release check (the version comparison, the channel selection, the rate-limit and 404 error mapping are all still useful) but end at an informational banner that deep-links to TestFlight via itms-beta:// or the public TestFlight invitation URL, where the user installs the update. The https-in-code and host-allowlist hardening becomes unnecessary because no executable is fetched. Add a TestFlight-specific concern Android does not have: TestFlight builds expire 90 days after upload, so the app should surface its own expiry date and prompt for an update before it stops launching.

impossible.capability: Wear APK update checking, download and push to the watch (WearAppUpdateChecker, WearApkPusher, WatchFaceInstaller)
impossible.why: watchOS has no sideloading. A watchOS app is a target inside the iOS app bundle and is installed by the system through the Watch app; there is no API by which the iPhone app can transfer and install an executable on the paired Watch. The watchface APK push is doubly impossible because watchOS has no third-party custom watch faces at all.
impossible.closest_alternative: Nothing is needed — the capability dissolves. The Watch app ships in the same TestFlight build as the iPhone app and installs automatically (or via the Watch app's toggle), so watch and phone versions cannot diverge and the entire channel/version/dev-build-number comparison machinery, the 100 MB cap, the push flow and the optimistic 15-second 'Success' state are all deleted. The watch-face capability's closest substitute is WidgetKit complications on Apple's system faces plus Smart Stack widgets, configured from the iPhone app — this is another subsystem's problem, but the watchface_* settings keys in AppSettingsStore should be repurposed to complication/widget configuration rather than ported.

ios_requirements: All pump, CGM, bolus, basal, battery, reservoir, alert, raw-history and outbound-queue data must be stored in a single encrypted local database that remains readable while the device is locked, so that background monitoring, alerting and upload continue after the screen turns off.

The database encryption key must be generated once on first run, be readable only by this app on this device and only after the device has been unlocked at least once since boot, and the app must refuse to open the database rather than mint a second key and orphan existing data.
A fresh installation must not inherit auth tokens, pump pairing secrets or database keys left behind in the system keychain by a previous installation of the same app.

The local store must reject duplicates at write time: at most one CGM reading per timestamp, one basal reading per timestamp, one bolus per (units, timestamp) pair, and one raw-history record per pump sequence number.
When a cloud-sourced record and a pump-sourced record collide on the same timestamp, resolution must be deterministic and documented: first writer wins for CGM and basal, last writer wins for bolus.
Stored rows that violate current safety invariants — glucose outside 20–500 mg/dL, bolus units outside 0–25 U — must be skipped when read and never displayed, uploaded, or used for alerting.

Glucose must be stored, transported, compared and threshold-tested in mg/dL everywhere; mmol/L must exist only as a display conversion using the single canonical constant, converted once from the most precise mg/dL value and rounded to one decimal last, with a dot decimal separator regardless of the device's locale.
The user must be able to choose a data-retention window between 1 and 30 days, defaulting to 7, and the app must enforce it without the user having to open any particular screen.
Retention must bound the alert history and the raw pump-history table as well as the six pump-data tables, so no table can grow without limit.

Every uploadable pump event must be durably recorded locally before any upload is attempted, and must survive app suspension, app termination and device restart until the backend accepts it or retention drops it.
An upload that begins while the app is in the foreground must be able to complete after the user backgrounds the app, without requiring the app to keep running.

Upload failures must be classified so that transport failures and HTTP 408, 429, 502, 503 and 504 never consume an event's retry budget, while other non-2xx responses do consume it so that a permanently rejected batch is eventually dropped rather than blocking every newer event behind it.

The outbound queue must be bounded, and when the bound is exceeded the oldest undelivered events must be dropped; the bound must be sized so that a full day without a successful upload does not discard data.
The user must be able to see how many events are waiting to upload and when the last successful upload happened, and that pending count must not be misleading while an upload is in flight.

Removing the server URL must leave a fully functional local-only monitor: no undelivered upload rows are retained, no backend request is attempted, local alert thresholds can be set on the device, and the on-device alert floor is the sole alerting path and is described as such.
Adding a server URL must resume syncing without requiring an app restart, and signing out must preserve both the server URL and the queued events so they drain on the next successful sign-in.

The app must attempt queue drain, retention, alert-threshold refresh and cloud-source sync at every execution opportunity the system grants it — app activation, Bluetooth wake, scheduled background refresh, background-upload completion — rather than on a fixed interval, and retry eligibility must be computed from stored timestamps so that an irregular schedule delays delivery without losing or corrupting an event.

The app must state, both inside the app and on a Lock Screen or Home Screen surface, whether anything is currently watching for lows and highs, and that statement must fail toward 'not watching' rather than going stale, optimistic, or silent.

The app must never claim background coverage it cannot deliver: when monitoring has stopped because the iPhone was restarted, the app was force-quit, Bluetooth is off, Local Network access was denied, or notifications are not authorized, the user must be told which one and what to do about it.

Onboarding must tell the user explicitly that restarting the iPhone or force-quitting the app stops monitoring until the app is opened again, and that background data collection is best-effort and may miss readings.

The initial multi-month pump history download must run as a user-visible, cancellable, resumable foreground task with accurate progress, resuming from the last downloaded record rather than restarting, and must keep the screen awake while it runs.

The user must stay signed in across app restarts; the access token must be refreshed before it expires whenever the app has execution time, and specifically before any upload is handed to the system for deferred delivery.
A 401 response must trigger exactly one serialized refresh-and-retry shared across all concurrent requests, so a refresh token is never rotated twice concurrently.
Signing out must always win over any in-flight token refresh; a refresh that completes after sign-out must never restore a session.

A session that expires while offline must show 'session expired, sign in again' without erasing the server URL, the user's email address, or any local pump history, and must not block the user from viewing local data or the on-device alert floor from arming.

The app must refuse plaintext HTTP to any host that is not a literal loopback, private, carrier-NAT or link-local IP address or a .local name, enforced both when the URL is saved and again on every request, classifying by literal address only and never by DNS resolution.

Reaching a server on the local network must request Local Network access, and a denial must be surfaced to the user as a permission problem with a route to Settings, never as a generic connection failure.

The user must be able to opt in to insecure LAN HTTP explicitly; that choice is per-device and must survive sign-out. Using a private certificate authority over https must be documented as the preferred alternative.

The app must report three distinct connectivity states — device offline, backend unreachable, reachable — with device-offline taking precedence, flipping to unreachable only after two consecutive transport failures, and excluding both cancelled requests and long-running AI inference calls from that signal.

The app must be able to sound an urgent-low or urgent-high alarm while the iPhone is silenced or in a Focus mode; if that capability has not been granted, the app must say plainly that alarms will not sound while the phone is silenced rather than presenting itself as armed.

The on-device alert floor must never alarm off a reading whose own sensor timestamp is older than the freshness bound, off thresholds that were never configured, or while the device clock has moved backwards; the same freshness predicate must gate both the phone alarm and the wrist relay, with no second definition anywhere.

A backend response carrying alert thresholds, a target glucose range, or safety limits that fails validation must be dropped, never clamped, leaving the last known-good values in place; ordering must be validated on the raw server values before any rounding.

The user must be able to acknowledge an alert with no network connection; the acknowledgement must stick locally, silence the alarm immediately, and be reconciled with the server exactly once when connectivity returns, and a re-delivered server alert must never re-alarm something the user already acknowledged offline.
An ongoing low or high must continue to reach the wrist until the episode ends or is acknowledged, and must never be retracted to an 'all clear' on data the app cannot vouch for.

The Apple Watch app must show current glucose, trend, time since the last reading, insulin on board, and the same coverage claim the iPhone shows, and must age its own copy out on its own clock rather than presenting an unbounded-stale value as current.
The Apple Watch app must ship in the same build as the iPhone app; there must be no separate watch update, watch install, or watch face installation flow.

The app must tell the user when a newer build is available and route them to the distribution channel to install it, and must never download or install executable code itself; the app must also surface its own build expiry so the user updates before it stops launching.

The app must never issue any command that changes pump therapy; the pump interface must expose read-only status queries only, and this must be enforced by the module's public interface, not by convention.

The app must include a compile-time-linked simulated pump driver and an in-app fault-injection surface — inject a CGM reading, force the backend unreachable, accelerate staleness — so that persistence, sync, retry classification, alert floor, wrist relay and the coverage claim can all be exercised in the iOS Simulator with no physical pump present.
Release builds must offer a user-accessible diagnostic log export, scrubbed of tokens, email addresses and glucose values, because the platform gives users no way to read the app's system log.

The app must tolerate unknown fields in every backend response and must apply the documented default for every absent optional field rather than failing to decode the response, and must accept backend timestamps with or without fractional seconds.
The app must register itself with the backend as an iOS device with a stable per-installation identifier and deregister on sign-out; registration failure must never block use of the app.

risks.risk: Core Bluetooth does not exist in the iOS Simulator at all — CBCentralManager reports .unsupported. Every capability downstream of pump BLE (polling cadence, persistence, enqueue, alert floor, wrist relay, coverage claim) is unreachable in the Simulator unless a substitute source exists. This is the single largest constraint on the stated Mac-plus-Simulator development loop.
risks.mitigation: Make the compile-time-linked driver interface substitutable and ship a SimulatedPumpDriver as a first-class target from day one, driving realistic CGM/basal/bolus/IoB streams including warmup, signal-loss (same sensor timestamp returned repeatedly), clock skew and disconnect. The Android build already proves this pattern works — BleDebugViewModel.injectTestCgm is explicitly the production-path test seam. Everything except the BLE transport itself can then be developed and regression-tested in the Simulator; reserve a physical iPhone plus pump only for driver work.

risks.risk: Background poll cadence cannot be guaranteed. The 15-second fast loop exists because the pump drops idle BLE connections at roughly 30 seconds; a suspended iOS app cannot issue the host-initiated request that keeps it alive. If the pump protocol has no peripheral-initiated notify characteristic, the background experience degrades to reconnect-driven wakes and the iPhone will capture materially fewer readings than the Android build.
risks.mitigation: Determine early — in the BLE subsystem — whether the pump notifies. Adopt CBCentralManager state restoration plus a permanently pending connect() so iOS re-establishes and wakes the app whenever the peripheral reappears. Measure real overnight capture rate on a device before committing to any freshness promise in the product copy, and make the coverage surface report actual reading age rather than an assumed cadence.

risks.risk: Server-generated alerts cannot reach a backgrounded iPhone at all today. The backend contract has no APNs endpoint (verified), and iOS cannot hold the SSE stream open while suspended. Without new push infrastructure, the on-device floor is the ONLY background alerting on iOS — a strictly weaker posture than Android, where the SSE foreground service delivers server alerts continuously.
risks.mitigation: Resolve the push question (see questions_for_pm) before scoping alerting. In the interim, run SSE foreground-only, pull pending alerts at every execution opportunity, and be explicit in the UI and onboarding that server alerts arrive only when the app is open.

risks.risk: Alarming through silent mode and Focus requires the Critical Alerts entitlement, which Apple grants only by approved request and ties to the developer account. Without it, an urgent-low alarm is inaudible whenever the ringer switch is off — a silent-floor failure of exactly the kind GLY-115/116 exist to prevent.
risks.mitigation: Apply for com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts as an early, tracked launch dependency. Ship the Time Sensitive interruption level as the fallback and make the honesty surface state which mode is active. Never present the app as armed for urgent lows while only Time Sensitive is available.

risks.risk: After an iPhone restart or a user force-quit, no code runs and monitoring silently stops with no way for the app to notice or notify. The Android BootCompletedReceiver has no substitute.
risks.mitigation: Explicit onboarding copy, a Home Screen widget whose displayed data age makes the stopped state visually obvious, and — if push is adopted — a server-side watchdog that pushes when a device stops reporting, which is the only mechanism that can relaunch the app without the user.

risks.risk: Data Protection and Keychain accessibility misconfiguration would make the database and the auth token unreadable whenever the device is locked, killing background writes and the alert floor — and the iOS Simulator does not enforce file data protection or device-lock keychain semantics, so this failure is invisible in the development loop and only appears on a locked physical device.
risks.mitigation: Standardise on kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly and FileProtectionType.completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication, assert both at startup, and add a device-only test that locks the screen and verifies a background write succeeds. Treat any Simulator-only validation of this area as no validation at all.

risks.risk: Local Network permission behaves differently in the Simulator than on device: the Simulator uses the Mac's network stack and does not enforce the privacy prompt, so a LAN-hosted backend will work perfectly in development and fail with opaque connection errors on a real iPhone.
risks.mitigation: Add NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription, an explicit permission pre-flight with a distinct user-facing error and a Settings deep link, and make LAN connectivity a mandatory on-device test before any release. Recommend private-CA https in the setup documentation as the path that avoids the whole class of problem.

risks.risk: Background execution behaviour is essentially unverifiable in the Simulator. BGTaskScheduler tasks only run when manually triggered from the debugger, background URLSession does not realistically survive suspension, Live Activity lifecycle limits do not apply, and ProcessInfo low-power mode and battery level are absent (batteryLevel returns -1).
risks.mitigation: Design every background path to be independently invokable from a debug menu so the logic can be tested in the Simulator, and schedule recurring on-device soak tests (overnight, locked, low-power mode on) as the only real validation of the background model.

risks.risk: Swift Codable does not apply a property's default value when a JSON key is absent, whereas Moshi's Kotlin adapter does. Fields such as is_automated, acknowledged, raw_accepted, raw_duplicates and source would fail to decode if the backend omits them — turning a tolerated absence on Android into a hard parse failure on iOS, potentially failing an entire alert or push response.
risks.mitigation: Decode every defaulted field with decodeIfPresent and an explicit default, and extend the contract smoke test to assert that every field carrying a default decodes correctly when absent from the payload — this assertion does not exist on Android because it cannot fail there.

risks.risk: Distribution risk: an unofficial third-party application that reads a commercial insulin pump and presents glucose data is subject to App Review guideline 1.4.1 and receives additional scrutiny; TestFlight external testing requires Beta App Review, and rejection would remove the intended distribution channel. TestFlight builds also expire 90 days after upload.
risks.mitigation: Position the app unambiguously as a read-only monitoring companion with a prominent medical disclaimer, ship the existing MEDICAL-DISCLAIMER content in-app, and never expose anything that could read as therapy control. Consider internal TestFlight distribution (up to 100 testers on the team, no Beta App Review) as a lower-risk starting posture, and build automated release cadence so the 90-day expiry never strands testers.

risks.risk: Background URLSession supports only file-backed upload and download tasks and may be marked discretionary by the system, so a queued pump-event batch can be deferred for a long time and must carry a token that will still be valid when it eventually runs.
risks.mitigation: Serialize each batch to a temp file, refresh the access token as a precondition of handing an upload to the system, keep the batch under the contract's 100-event maximum, and make the server-side dedup (which already reports accepted/duplicates) the safety net for a batch that runs twice.

risks.risk: WatchConnectivity delivery is best-effort with real budgets — high-priority complication transfers are limited to roughly 50 per day — so the relay's 5-minute silent refresh and 30-minute rebuzz cannot rely on the phone-to-watch channel to reach the wrist reliably.
risks.mitigation: Deliver wrist ALERTS as iPhone notifications mirrored to the Watch rather than as relayed data items, use updateApplicationContext (unbudgeted, coalesced) for state, and let the Watch decay its own copy so a missed update degrades to 'stale' rather than to a wrong value presented as current.

risks.risk: Packaging SQLCipher with Swift Package Manager is historically awkward because it requires custom compilation flags; the well-trodden path is CocoaPods, which adds a second dependency manager to the project.
risks.mitigation: Evaluate SQLCipher-via-SPM early and, if it does not build cleanly, either vendor a pre-configured SQLCipher SPM target or accept CocoaPods for that one dependency. Confirm the ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption declaration is present so TestFlight uploads are not blocked on export-compliance questions.

risks.risk: Camera is unavailable in the iOS Simulator, so meal-photo capture and the multipart vision upload cannot be exercised there; the photo picker with the simulated library is the only partial substitute.
risks.mitigation: Route meal capture through an abstraction that can be fed a bundled test image in the Simulator, so the compression, multipart-upload and error paths are testable without a camera.

questions_for_pm: Server-generated alerts cannot reach a backgrounded iPhone over the existing SSE stream — only APNs can, and APNs tokens are scoped to the app's bundle identifier, which means only the team that signs the TestFlight build can mint a valid push key. A self-hoster therefore cannot push to a project-signed app with their own key. Which trust model do we accept: (a) the project operates a small relay that self-hosted backends post alerts through, with the project holding the APNs key and seeing alert metadata; (b) the project distributes its APNs signing key to self-hosters, accepting that anyone holding it can push arbitrary alerts to every install; (c) users build and sign the app with their own Apple Developer team, which forecloses TestFlight distribution; or (d) we ship with no background server alerts at all and the on-device floor is the only background alerting on iOS, documented as a known regression from Android?
